A Multivariate Network Traffic Forecasting Method Based on Adaptive Multiscale Weighting

Hourly forecasting of backbone network traffic requires consideration of both short-term fluctuations and long-term trends. A lightweight adaptive multiscale forecasting model is therefore developed. Historical windows are represented at three temporal resolutions, and independent decomposition linear experts generate candidate forecasts. A routing network extracts four statistics from the current window: overall level, dispersion, final-time state, and mean absolute change. A two-layer perceptron uses these statistics to calculate fusion weights. Experiments on Abilene and GÉANT use 96 historical steps to predict the next 24 steps. Across three common random seeds, the proposed method reduces mean squared error by 4.07% and 4.54% relative to the single-scale decomposition linear model, respectively. The corresponding reductions relative to the sampling-oriented lightweight model

are 29.80% and 46.89%. Further ablation experiments across eight random seeds compare the proposed method with learned global weights and a constant-input router. On Abilene, the mean seed-wise improvements over both controls are approximately 1.80%; on GÉANT, they are 4.31% and 4.97%, respectively. The results show that combining multiscale candidate forecasts with low-dimensional routing achieves lower mean forecasting errors with few additional fusion parameters. The forecasts can provide a reference for next-day network traffic demand analysis and capacity planning.
